prompt.context: The authorities of the Mexico City airport have decided to issue 2,500 new taxi permits for $1,000 each. These permits authorize a taxi to service arriving passengers. Your client has a taxi fleet in the city but does not service the airport. He has excess capacity (meaning he has cars and drivers available). He has asked you to determine if he should buy those new permits. If so, how many should he buy?
prompt.question: Should the client buy any of the 2,500 new airport taxi permits at $1,000 each? If so, how many should he buy?

clarifying_info.q: How many passengers does the airport handle?
clarifying_info.a: The airport handles 42 million passengers yearly.

clarifying_info.q: How many taxis are currently operating at the airport?
clarifying_info.a: There are 5,500 taxis currently operating at the airport.

clarifying_info.q: How long does a typical taxi trip take?
clarifying_info.a: On average a taxi takes 60 minutes to drive a passenger and return to the airport for the next pick-up.
On average a passenger pays $200 cab fare via regulated rates.

clarifying_info.q: What share of passengers use taxis?
clarifying_info.a: On average 40% of domestic flight passengers and 80% of international flight passengers use taxis.

clarifying_info.q: How is demand distributed throughout the day?
clarifying_info.a: 30% of daily demand occurs between 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m., 40% occurs between 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., and the remaining 30% occurs during other hours.
Assume each passenger uses one cab.
On average each taxi requires $8,000 yearly on maintenance.
Taxi drivers keep 50% of the fare.

clarifying_info.q: What is the domestic vs. international passenger split?
clarifying_info.a: Assume 50% of passengers are from domestic flights and 50% from international flights.

clarifying_info.q: Is passenger volume evenly distributed through the year?
clarifying_info.a: Assume that passenger volume is equally distributed through the year, week, and day.

exhibits.title: Mexico City Airport Taxi Facts & Assumptions
exhibits.shows: A fact sheet listing key data about the Mexico City airport taxi market, including annual passenger volume, number of existing taxis, average trip duration, regulated fare, taxi usage rates by flight type, peak demand time windows, and cost/revenue sharing assumptions.
exhibits.data: Airport handles 42 million passengers yearly; 5,500 taxis operating; 60-minute average round trip; $200 average fare (regulated); 40% domestic passengers use taxis, 80% international passengers use taxis; 30% of daily demand 6am-10am, 40% of daily demand 6pm-10pm; each passenger uses one cab; $8,000 yearly maintenance per taxi; drivers keep 50% of fare

framework: P = R - C: Frame the problem as a profitability analysis
Revenue side: estimate daily and annual taxi demand, identify unmet demand (gap between capacity and demand), calculate revenue per taxi and in total
Cost side: identify all relevant costs — permit purchase price, annual maintenance, driver commissions (salary)
Demand analysis: estimate daily arriving passengers, segment by domestic/international, apply taxi usage rates, determine peak vs. off-peak demand and compare to current capacity
Profit calculation: multiply unmet demand by revenue per trip, subtract costs, determine net profit
Decision: recommend how many permits to buy based on profitable unmet demand

questions.prompt: Estimate the number of passengers arriving at the airport each day.
questions.guidance: A strong answer breaks annual volume down to daily: 42M / 12 months = 3.5M monthly; / 4 weeks = 875,000 weekly; / 7 days = 125,000 daily. Candidate should note the simplifying assumption of equal distribution.

math.setup: 42,000,000 annual passengers divided down to daily figure

questions.prompt: Estimate how many of those daily passengers will require a taxi.
questions.guidance: Candidate must split 50/50 domestic vs. international and apply the respective taxi-usage rates. 62,500 domestic x 40% + 62,500 international x 80% = 25,000 + 50,000 = 75,000 taxi-demanding passengers per day.

math.setup: Split 125,000 daily passengers 50/50 by flight type, then apply usage rates
math.answer: 75,000 passengers demand a taxi each day

questions.prompt: Estimate daily demand by time period and determine whether current supply of 5,500 taxis meets that demand. How many additional taxis are needed?
questions.guidance: Break demand into three windows: morning peak 30% = 22,500; evening peak 40% = 30,000; off-peak 30% = 22,500. Each taxi does 1 trip/hour (60-min cycle). Morning peak (4 hours): 5,500 taxis x 4 trips = 22,000 capacity vs 22,500 demand → 500 unmet. Evening peak (4 hours): same 22,000 capacity vs 30,000 demand → 8,000 unmet. Off-peak (16 hours): 5,500 x 16 = 88,000 capacity vs 22,500 → excess capacity. For morning gap: 500 passengers / 4 trips per hour = 125 taxis needed. For evening gap: 8,000 passengers / 4 trips = 2,000 taxis needed. Total new taxis needed = 2,000 (the evening peak drives the constraint).

math.setup: Each time window: demand = 75,000 x share; capacity = 5,500 taxis x hours in window (1 trip/hour)
steps: Morning capacity: 5,500 x 4 = 22,000 → excess demand = 500 passengers → 500/4 = 125 taxis needed
Evening capacity: 5,500 x 4 = 22,000 → excess demand = 8,000 passengers → 8,000/4 = 2,000 taxis needed
Off-peak demand: 75,000 x 30% = 22,500; capacity = 5,500 x 16 = 88,000 → surplus
Total additional taxis required to meet all unmet demand: 2,000 (driven by evening peak)
math.answer: 2,000 additional taxis are needed to meet unmet demand (125 in morning, 2,000 in evening — evening is binding)

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual profit from buying 2,000 permits and operating 2,000 taxis at the airport.
questions.guidance: Revenue: 8,500 unmet passengers per day x $200 fare x 336 operating days (or use 365 days simplification) — casebook uses 8,500 x $200 = $1,700,000 daily and x 336 days = $571,200,000 yearly. Client keeps 50% of fare so revenue to client = $571,200,000 / 2... actually casebook treats full fare as revenue and driver commission as cost. Costs: maintenance $8,000 x 2,000 = $16,000,000; driver commissions 50% x $571,200,000 = $285,600,000; permit cost $1,000 x 2,000 = $2,000,000. Profit = $571,200,000 - $16,000,000 - $285,600,000 - $2,000,000 = $267,600,000.

math.setup: Annual profit = Yearly Revenue - Maintenance - Driver Commissions - Permit Costs
steps: Permit cost (one-time, treated in year 1): $1,000 x 2,000 = $2,000,000

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or additional considerations should the client weigh before deciding how many permits to buy?

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: Other taxi companies may buy remaining 500 permits and compete for the same excess demand
Competitors could retaliate by entering markets where the client currently operates
No guarantee the airport will not issue additional permits in the future, increasing competition

categories.name: Demand risk
ideas: Not all 2,000 new taxis will necessarily capture all unmet demand — passengers may use other transport
Demand assumptions (50/50 domestic/international split, equal daily distribution) may not hold

categories.name: Operational considerations
ideas: Client must ensure drivers and cars are available specifically during peak windows (6am-10am and 6pm-10pm)
Maintenance timing must not conflict with peak service hours

categories.name: Strategic option — buy all 2,500 permits
ideas: Buying all 2,500 permits (using 2,000 taxis) blocks competitors from the remaining 500 permits
Profit impact: $267,600,000 - $500,000 (extra permit cost) = $267,100,000 — still highly profitable
This defensive move may be worth the small reduction in profit

recommendation: The client should buy 2,000 permits at a cost of $2,000,000, yielding an estimated annual profit of $267,600,000 from servicing unmet airport taxi demand driven primarily by the evening peak period (6pm-10pm).
Alternatively, buying all 2,500 permits (blocking competitors) reduces profit only marginally to ~$267,100,000 and may be the preferred strategic choice.
risks: Competitors could buy the remaining 500 permits and compete directly for the same unmet demand
Airport authorities may issue additional permits in the future, diluting margins
Retaliation: competitors may enter the client's existing city markets
Actual unmet demand may be lower if passengers use rideshare or other transport alternatives
next_steps: Assess whether to purchase all 2,500 permits defensively
Evaluate driver availability and logistics for peak-hour deployment (6am-10am and 6pm-10pm)
Monitor airport permit policy for future issuance plans
Track actual passenger taxi uptake after launch to validate demand assumptions
